featured.name: pi-hashline-edit-pro
featured.headline: Edits that land on the line you meant
summary: Line numbers drift the moment anything above them changes, and fuzzy matching quietly does the worst possible thing when it half-matches. pi-hashline-edit-pro removes both failure modes: every line gets a unique 4-character anchor, and the anchor is the only address an edit can use.

It registers read, replace, insert, anchor_grep, and undo_last_change, and disables the built-in edit tool. In its own benchmark it leads the field at 86% overall correctness and 96.3% on stale-and-drift scenarios.

points.title: Anchors survive edits
points.body: Anchors are content-addressed, so inserting or deleting lines never renumbers the ones you did not touch. Follow-up edits keep working without a re-read.

points.title: Stale edits are refused
points.body: Every served row is remembered. If the file changed underneath, the tool answers [E_RANGE_STALE] with the current range and fresh anchors instead of silently editing a neighbor.

points.title: Undo is byte-exact
points.body: The last replace or insert on a file reverts with BOM and line endings intact, and the history survives a session restart.

points.title: Batches are atomic
points.body: Multiple edits group per file into one batch with a combined diff and a single undo. Overlaps, or one stale member, abort the whole batch unwritten.

principles: Show the model what it sees
about: I build tools for coding agents, mostly extensions for pi. The pattern behind every one of them is the same: find something agents get subtly wrong, then make the wrong version impossible.

The packages are all on npm. The flagship anchors every line with a 4-character hash so edits cannot drift, refuses stale edits instead of guessing, and has an undo that restores bytes. When I wanted proof it was better, I built the benchmark and published the traces.
Everything on this page is real data. Numbers refresh daily from the GitHub and npm APIs through a scheduled workflow, and the benchmark figures are read from committed run reports.
